config.title: Winter Tyres in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: When Berlin roads actually start freezing, what the Alpine symbol changed, what the wrong tyres cost in fines and insurance, and who has to grit the pavement outside your door.

items.q: When do I legally need winter tyres in Berlin?
items.a: There is no date. Germany has a situational requirement in § 2 Absatz 3a StVO: your car must be on winter-capable tyres whenever the road has black ice, packed snow, slush, ice or Reifglätte, which is frost slickness. That means the trigger is the condition of the road on the morning you drive, not the month on the calendar. The saying von O bis O, October to Easter, is a memory aid invented by the motoring clubs and has no legal force, although October is a sensible deadline to treat it as.

items.q: When does the road in Berlin actually start freezing?
items.a: Earlier than most people think. The Deutscher Wetterdienst records a minimum temperature 5 cm above the ground as well as the standard air minimum at 2 m, and ground frost can occur while the measured air temperature is still 3 to 5 °C. Across the thirty winters from 1995/96 to 2024/25 at the Berlin-Tempelhof station, the median date of the first ground frost is 30 September and the median date of the first air frost is 6 November, a median gap of 35 days. In 16 of those 30 winters the first ground frost fell in September, the earliest on 17 September. The first air frost has never arrived before 18 October in that record.

items.q: What is the Alpine symbol and why does it matter now?
items.a: It is a pictogram of a mountain with a snowflake inside it, moulded into the tyre sidewall, officially called 3PMSF. Since 1 October 2024 it is the only marking that makes a tyre count as a winter tyre in German winter conditions. The older M+S marking on its own stopped being enough when the transition period for tyres produced before 2018 ended on 30 September 2024. If your winter set is around eight years old or more, check the sidewall before the first cold morning.

items.q: Are all-season tyres legal in Berlin?
items.a: Yes, provided they carry the Alpine symbol. All-season tyres with 3PMSF satisfy the situational winter tyre requirement exactly like dedicated winter tyres. For a car that mostly does short trips inside the S-Bahn ring they are usually the practical choice. If you regularly drive out into Brandenburg in winter or take the Autobahn south, a proper winter set is the better buy.

items.q: What does driving on summer tyres in winter cost in Germany?
items.a: Driving on unsuitable tyres in winter conditions is 60 euros and one point in Flensburg. If you obstruct other traffic it is 80 euros, and if you endanger someone it is 100 euros, each with the point. The registered keeper can be fined separately for allowing it. The bigger risk is insurance: your compulsory third-party cover still pays the other party, but the insurer can claim up to 5,000 euros back from you in Regress, and a Kasko policy can cut or refuse payment for your own car on the grounds of gross negligence unless the contract waives that objection.

items.q: How much tread do winter tyres need?
items.a: The legal minimum for any tyre in Germany is 1.6 mm, which is a poor target for winter driving. The ADAC recommends replacing winter tyres once they reach 4 mm, because grip on snow and wet drops away quickly below that. Age matters as well: the rubber hardens, so a set that has done six or seven seasons can pass a tread check and still behave badly in the cold. The four-digit DOT code on the sidewall gives the week and year of manufacture.

items.q: What does a tyre change cost in Berlin?
items.a: Swapping wheels that already sit on their own rims runs roughly 20 to 50 euros for all four. Mounting and balancing four tyres onto existing rims is more like 40 to 80 euros, and more again for large rims or heavy SUV wheels. Seasonal storage, which most Berlin flats need because there is no cellar space, starts around 39 euros in the city and averages closer to 70 for four wheels. Prices and waiting times both rise in the October and November peak, so book early.

items.q: Which Berlin roads get gritted first?
items.a: The BSR runs the winter service with around 540 vehicles, about 13,000 tonnes of salt and 5,000 tonnes of grit, and works to a fixed order: city motorways and main traffic routes first, then roads carrying buses and trams, cycle lanes and pedestrian crossings. Residential side streets come last. Bridges and flyovers freeze before the roads on either side because cold air reaches them from underneath, which is why a quiet, shaded side street and a bridge are the two places a car on summer tyres finds out.

items.q: Who has to clear the pavement outside a Berlin building?
items.a: The property owner, although the duty is very often transferred to tenants in the lease, so check your contract before the first cold week. The strip has to be cleared and gritted from 07:00 Monday to Saturday and from 09:00 on Sundays and public holidays until 20:00, and promptly once snowfall stops or ice forms outside those hours. The cleared width is 1.5 m on the busiest cleaning classes and at least 1 m elsewhere. De-icing salt is banned for private use in Berlin, so use sand, grit or granulate. A breach is an administrative offence with a fine that can reach 10,000 euros, and an injured pedestrian is a separate civil claim.
